tips.title: Every one of them takes an infinitive
tips.body: **Il faut**, **on doit**, **on devrait**, **on pourrait**, **il vaut mieux**, **il est important de** — each followed by an **infinitive** that never changes. One word to get right instead of a conjugation, which makes them the safest structures under pressure. (*Il faut* can also take a noun, *il me faut du temps*, but the infinitive is the use you need here.)},

tips.title: Prefer devrait to doit
tips.body: Where either would fit, use **on devrait** rather than *on doit*. It means *should* rather than *must*, and it is the **conditional**, so it shows a tense your present-only sentences do not. Same effort, more credit.

tips.title: Ne … que means only
tips.body: *Ne … pas*, *ne … plus*, *ne … rien* and *ne … jamais* are negatives, but **ne … que** means **only**. *Je ne prends que le bus* is *I only take the bus*. Reading it as a negative reverses the sentence.

tips.title: Which si pattern does the sentence want?
tips.body: **Si + present, + future** makes a prediction: *Si on ne fait rien, la situation sera pire.* **Si + imperfect, + conditional** makes a hypothesis: *Si tout le monde recyclait, il y aurait moins de déchets.* Decide which you mean before choosing the tense.

steps.title: Ce que je fais
steps.body:
Start with what **you** already do, in the present tense. These are the actions that come up most, and most of them are regular **-er** verbs, so they are easy to get right.

- **recycler** — to recycle: *Je recycle le verre et le papier.*
- **trier les déchets** — to sort the rubbish
- **économiser l'eau / l'énergie** — to save water / energy
- **éteindre la lumière** — to turn off the light (irregular: *j'éteins*)
- **prendre le bus** — to take the bus (*je prends*)
- **aller au collège à pied / à vélo** — to walk / cycle to school
- **éviter le plastique** — to avoid plastic
- **réutiliser** — to reuse

Two useful additions that cost nothing and earn a lot:

- a **frequency** word: *toujours, souvent, tous les jours, une fois par semaine, rarement*
- a **reason**: *parce que c'est important pour la planète*

> *Je recycle **toujours** le verre **parce que** c'est facile.*

That is three marks' worth from one action.

check.prompt: Traduis en français : I always recycle glass.
check.solution: **Je recycle toujours le verre.** A **single-word** frequency adverb goes **after** the verb in French, not before it as in English. Phrases such as *tous les jours* or *une fois par semaine* go at the **start or the end** of the sentence instead: *Je trie le verre **tous les jours***.

steps.title: Il faut, on doit, on devrait
steps.body:
To say what **should** be done, you need a small set of structures, and they all share one rule: **every one is followed by an infinitive**.

- **il faut** — you have to, one must
- **on doit** — we must
- **on devrait** — we should
- **on pourrait** — we could
- **il est important de** — it is important to
- **il vaut mieux** — it is better to

> *Il faut **recycler** plus.*
> *On devrait **utiliser** moins de plastique.*
> *Il est important de **trier** les déchets.*

The infinitive never changes, whatever the subject. That is what makes these structures so useful under pressure: one word to get right instead of a conjugation.

**On doit** and **on devrait** are worth separating carefully. *On doit* is **must**, a duty. *On devrait* is **should**, a recommendation, and it is the **conditional** of *devoir*. Using *on devrait* shows a tense the present-only answer does not have, so prefer it when either would do.

Note that **il est important de** and **il vaut mieux** differ: *important* needs **de** before the infinitive, *il vaut mieux* does not.

steps.title: Les actions collectives
steps.body:
Individual actions are worth marks; **collective** actions are worth more, because they let you talk about the town, the school or the government rather than only yourself.

- **la mairie** — the town hall, the council
- **le gouvernement** — the government
- **une association** — a charity, a campaign group
- **une piste cyclable** — a cycle path
- **les transports en commun** — public transport
- **une zone piétonne** — a pedestrian zone
- **interdire** — to ban (*on a interdit*, it has been banned)
- **construire** — to build
- **planter des arbres** — to plant trees
- **organiser une collecte** — to organise a collection

These combine naturally with the **passive** and with **on**:

> *On **a construit** une nouvelle piste cyclable.*
> *Les sacs en plastique **ont été interdits**.*
> *La mairie **devrait** créer une zone piétonne.*

That last pattern — a named body plus *devrait* plus an infinitive — is the single most useful sentence in this topic, because it gives an opinion **and** a recommendation in one clause.

steps.title: Trois temps en trois phrases
steps.body: The highest-value habit in this topic is showing **what you used to do, what you do now, and what you will do**. It turns a list of actions into a piece of writing with range, and it needs no extra vocabulary.

steps.text: **Present**, what you do now: *Maintenant, je **trie** le verre, le papier et le plastique.*
**Future**, what you will do: *L'année prochaine, j'**essaierai** d'éviter le plastique.*
Add a reason to any one of them: *…, **parce que** je pense que c'est important.*

steps.title: Dire que ce n'est pas assez
steps.body:
An answer that only says what is being done sounds like a leaflet. The top band wants a **view**, which usually means saying that something is not enough, or that it will not work.

- **ce n'est pas assez** — that is not enough
- **ça ne suffit pas** — that is not sufficient
- **c'est un bon début, mais …** — it's a good start, but …
- **il reste beaucoup à faire** — there is a lot left to do
- **la plupart des gens ne font rien** — most people do nothing
- **à quoi ça sert si …** — what's the point if …

> *On a construit une piste cyclable, mais **ce n'est pas assez**, car la plupart des gens prennent toujours la voiture.*

Notice the negative structures. *Ne … rien* (nothing) and *ne … plus* (no longer) wrap around the verb exactly as *ne … pas* does:

> *Je **n'**utilise **plus** de sacs en plastique.* — I no longer use plastic bags.
> *La plupart des gens **ne** font **rien**.* — Most people do nothing.

After a negative, **du, de la, des** become **de**: *je n'utilise **plus de** sacs*, not *plus des sacs*. Two exceptions: not after **être** (*ce n'est pas **du** plastique*), and not after **ne … que**, which means *only* and is not really a negative (*je ne bois que **de l'**eau*).

steps.title: À toi : et toi, que fais-tu ?
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Traduis en français.

1. We should use less plastic.
2. The council should build a cycle path.
3. I no longer take the car.

**Partie B.** Réponds en français, en phrases complètes.

4. Que fais-tu pour protéger l'environnement ? Donne deux actions et une fréquence.
5. Que devrait faire ta ville ? Utilise *devrait* et un infinitif.
6. Est-ce que c'est assez ? Pourquoi ?

**Partie C.** Écris cinq phrases : ce que tu faisais avant, ce que tu fais maintenant, ce que tu feras, ce que la mairie devrait faire, et ton opinion sur ce qui est déjà fait.

For part C, use the time phrases — *avant*, *maintenant*, *l'année prochaine* — so the examiner can see which tense you meant.

steps.title: Aller plus loin: l'objection
steps.body:
The clearest way to lift this topic into the top band is to **raise an objection and answer it**. It shows two structures at once and reads like a real opinion rather than a set of good intentions.

> *Certains disent que les actions individuelles **ne servent à rien**, parce qu'une seule personne **ne peut pas** changer le climat. **Cependant**, je pense que si tout le monde **faisait** un petit effort, **on pourrait** vraiment changer les choses.*

That sentence contains: a reported view (*certains disent que*), a negative (*ne servent à rien*), a concession (*cependant*), an imperfect in a *si* clause, and a conditional (*on pourrait*). It is four structures in two sentences, and none of them is rare.

**The si pattern to learn here.** *Si* + **imperfect**, then **conditional**:

> *Si tout le monde **recyclait**, il y **aurait** moins de déchets.* — If everyone recycled, there would be less rubbish.

Compare it with the pattern from the problems topic, *si* + present + future: *Si on ne fait rien, la situation sera pire.* The two are different and both are useful. The imperfect–conditional one is hypothetical; the present–future one is a prediction.

**One warning.** *Ne … que* means **only**, not a negative: *Je **ne** prends **que** le bus* means *I only take the bus*, not *I don't take the bus*. Reading it as a negative reverses the meaning of the sentence, which is exactly the kind of trap a reading paper sets.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- Daily actions: **recycler**, **trier les déchets**, **économiser l'eau**, **éteindre la lumière**, **aller à pied / à vélo**, **éviter le plastique**.
- Add a **frequency** and a **reason** to every action: *Je recycle **toujours** le verre **parce que** c'est facile.*
- **Single-word** frequency adverbs go **after** the verb: *je recycle **toujours***. Longer phrases such as *tous les jours* go at the **start or end** of the sentence.
- **Il faut**, **on doit**, **on devrait**, **on pourrait**, **il est important de**, **il vaut mieux** — all followed by an **infinitive**, which never changes.
- **On devrait** is the conditional, meaning **should**; **on doit** means **must**. Prefer *devrait* when either fits, because it shows a tense.
- Collective action: **la mairie**, **le gouvernement**, **une association**, **une piste cyclable**, **les transports en commun**, **une zone piétonne**.
- The most useful sentence in the topic: a named body + **devrait** + infinitive.
- Negatives wrap around the verb: **ne … pas**, **ne … plus**, **ne … rien**, **ne … jamais**.
- After a negative, **du / de la / des** become **de** — but **not** after *être*, and **not** after *ne … que*, which is not really a negative.
- **Ne … que** means **only**, not a negative.
- **Si + present, + future** predicts. **Si + imperfect, + conditional** hypothesises.
- Raise an objection and answer it: *Certains disent que …, cependant …*

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

> ***Avant, je ne faisais pas** grand-chose pour l'environnement, parce que je trouvais ça compliqué. **Maintenant, je trie** le verre et le papier tous les jours, et je vais au collège à pied quand il ne pleut pas. **L'année prochaine, j'essaierai** d'éviter complètement le plastique, ce qui sera assez difficile. À mon avis, **la mairie devrait construire** plus de pistes cyclables, car beaucoup de gens n'osent pas faire du vélo en ville. On a interdit les sacs en plastique, ce qui est un bon début, **mais ça ne suffit pas**, car la plupart des gens prennent toujours la voiture.*

**What earns the marks.** Imperfect (*je ne faisais pas*), present (*je trie*), future (*j'essaierai*), conditional (*devrait*). Specific actions — glass, paper, walking — rather than *je protège l'environnement*. And an opinion with a **reservation**: *c'est un bon début, mais ça ne suffit pas*, which is worth more than simple approval.

questions.prompt: « Les actions individuelles ne servent à rien. » Es-tu d'accord ? Écris quatre phrases pour répondre.
questions.solution: Certains disent que les actions individuelles ne servent à rien, parce qu'une seule personne ne peut pas changer le climat. Je comprends cet argument, et c'est vrai que les grandes entreprises polluent beaucoup plus que nous. Cependant, je ne suis pas d'accord, car si tout le monde faisait un petit effort, il y aurait beaucoup moins de déchets. De plus, quand on change ses habitudes, on encourage les autres à faire la même chose, donc l'effet est plus grand qu'on ne le pense.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

> ***Certains disent que** les actions individuelles **ne servent à rien**, parce qu'une seule personne ne peut pas changer le climat. Je comprends cet argument, et **c'est vrai que** les grandes entreprises polluent beaucoup plus que nous. **Cependant**, je ne suis pas d'accord, car **si tout le monde faisait** un petit effort, **il y aurait** beaucoup moins de déchets. De plus, quand on change ses habitudes, on encourage les autres à faire la même chose, **donc** l'effet est plus grand qu'on ne le pense.*

**Why this scores.** It **concedes** before disagreeing (*c'est vrai que … cependant*), which shows balance and a conjunction. It uses **si + imperfect + conditional** (*faisait … aurait*), the hypothetical pattern. And it ends with a **reason of its own** rather than repeating the question.

examTechnique.body:
Name **specific** actions. *Je protège l'environnement* says nothing; *je trie le verre et le papier* says something, and adding *tous les jours* and *parce que c'est facile* turns one action into three marks.

Use the modal structures rather than conjugating: *on devrait*, *il faut*, *il est important de*, each with an infinitive.

Say what a **named body** should do — the council, the government, the school — as well as what you do. It widens the answer beyond yourself without new vocabulary.

Signal your tenses with time phrases: *avant*, *maintenant*, *l'année prochaine*. The examiner needs to see which tense you meant.

Do not end on approval. Say what is not enough, and why. A reservation is worth more than agreement.

Check your negatives wrap around the verb, and that *des* has become *de* after them.
examinerErrors: Conjugating after *on devrait* or *il faut*, which both need an infinitive.
Writing *je n'utilise plus des sacs*: after a negative *des* becomes *de*.
Reading *ne … que* as a negative, which reverses the meaning.
Putting a single-word frequency adverb before the verb, as in English.
Writing only about yourself, and never about what the town or the government should do.
Using *si* with the conditional in the first half; it is *si* + imperfect, then the conditional.
Giving vague intentions such as *je fais attention* instead of a specific action.
Ending on unqualified approval, where a reservation would score higher.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the question as an argument rather than a list. It names precise actions and attaches a frequency and a reason to each, then widens out to what the council or the government should do, using a modal with an infinitive. It moves through the tenses deliberately, marking each with a time phrase, and it reaches for *si* plus imperfect plus conditional when the idea is hypothetical. Above all it declines to be simply positive: it concedes that something has been done, says why it is not enough, and answers the obvious objection before the examiner can think of it.
